title: Skills in Weights, Memory in Code: Hybrid Learning for Memory-Dependent Robot Manipulation

visual_explainer.blocker: Two isolated GPT Image attempts on 2026-08-13 failed paper-specific Visual QA: the first rendered an unrelated GitHub repository dashboard with fabricated maintenance metadata; the second rendered a V-Mem explainer instead of HyMeS. Binary publication is available; the blocker is render grounding/identity.

analysis.tldr: HyMeS separates motor skills from memory strategy: a VLA learns reusable physical skills in weights, while a coding agent learns executable memory-management rules in code; symbolic task state then steers the frozen VLA's action denoising and is updated from multimodal execution feedback.
analysis.problem: Memory-dependent manipulation is non-Markovian: identical current observations can require different actions depending on earlier cues or counts. End-to-end memory-augmented VLAs can learn this, but they entangle memory logic with motor learning and require demonstrations that cover combinatorial history-dependent task states.
analysis.core_idea: Fine-tune a Markovian flow-matching VLA only for reusable motor skills, then use development rollouts to let a coding agent iteratively edit an executable program containing constraint-selection, event-verification, and memory-update rules. At runtime, the resulting symbolic memory selects a stage-specific differentiable constraint whose gradient steers VLA denoising; PACE verifies stage completion from proprioception plus multi-frame VLM evidence and updates memory.

memory_design.write: During development, rollout traces and stage-wise verdicts are used by a coding agent to revise the executable heuristic program. At episode start, the frozen program instantiates an initial symbolic task memory from the instruction and observation.
memory_design.organize: The program separates constraint-selection, event-verification, and update rules; runtime memory stores the plan, active stage, bindings, repetition counters, and persistent interaction state.
memory_design.read: The active symbolic state selects a differentiable stage constraint that is injected into the frozen flow-matching VLA's denoising process, so memory changes action-mode selection without changing policy weights.
memory_design.update_forget: PACE accepts stage-progress events using proprioceptive and multi-frame VLM judgments, then advances the stage and updates bindings/counters/persistent state. The learned program itself is frozen during evaluation; the paper does not study long-term forgetting.

compared_to: The same-weight reactive pi0.5 policy on the corrected RoboMemArena protocol
PrediMem reevaluated on the same corrected 12-task protocol
End-to-end memory-augmented VLAs that learn history-conditioned behavior in weight space from demonstrations
analysis.evidence: On a corrected 12-task/160-episode RoboMemArena protocol, HyMeS reports 66.2% cumulative success and 60.1% task success versus 52.5%/41.3% for pi0.5 and 61.7%/45.6% for PrediMem. On SO-101, task success rises from 25.7% to 57.1%. The paper reports that rollout experience adds +8.5 CSR and +18.4 TSR, and that combining proprioceptive and visual completion evidence is more reliable than either alone.
analysis.why_it_matters: HyMeS exposes a useful substrate boundary: long-horizon memory logic need not be baked into policy weights. Keeping motor competence in weights while putting inspectable, revisable task-state logic in code can reduce demonstration requirements and let memory directly steer action generation rather than merely orchestrate a high-level tool call.
limitations: The evaluation uses a corrected 12-task subset selected to isolate missing-history failures; although selection uses protocol checks and base-policy behavior rather than HyMeS results, broader RoboMemArena generality is not established.
Memory-strategy learning happens on development rollouts; the program is frozen at evaluation, so this is not continual online program evolution during deployment.
PACE depends partly on Qwen3-VL-8B completion judgments and hand-specified voting settings, creating another failure surface for memory updates.
Evidence covers one main VLA family and a small real-robot task set; transfer of learned code-space memory strategies across robots, policies, or open-ended tasks remains unclear.
